prompt: In `PropsBasics`, the second bar is written `<GoalBar label="Spanish" minutes="30" />`. What did `GoalBar` receive as `minutes`, and what did Vue do about it?
hint: Look at the line the component logged for Spanish.

choices.text: The number 30, because the prop is declared as a `Number`
choices.why: The declaration says what the child expects, not what it gets. Without the colon nothing converts the text.

choices.text: Nothing: Vue refused to render that bar
choices.why: The transcript shows `Spanish: 30 of 60 minutes` on the page. A failed check warns; it does not stop anything.

choices.text: The string `"30"`; Vue warned and used it
choices.why: Right. A plain attribute is text, the type check failed, and the bar still drew with the string: `minutes is a string`.

choices.text: `undefined`, because a prop passed without a colon is dropped
choices.why: It is not dropped; it arrives as text. `undefined` is what the fourth bar got for `label`, which was not passed at all.

prompt: In the `PropsBasics` transcript, how many `[Vue warn]` lines did the four bars produce?
hint: Three of the four uses were wrong.

prompt: Which of these are true of `defineProps`? Choose all that apply.
hint: It is read by the compiler before the code ever runs.

choices.text: It is used without being imported
choices.why: Right. It is a compiler macro, and the SFC compiler turns it into the component's options.

choices.text: It works only at the top level of `<script setup>`
choices.why: Right. The compiler looks for it there; inside a function it is not seen.

choices.text: A failed `validator` keeps the value out of the component
choices.why: `unit="days"` failed its validator and the bar still said `days`. A check in development warns and nothing more.

choices.text: A prop left out falls back to its `default`
choices.why: Right. `goal` was 60 on every bar that did not pass one.

choices.text: The array form `['label', 'minutes']` checks the types too
choices.why: The array form names the props and says nothing about their types; the object forms are the ones that check.

prompt: A child writes `const { done } = defineProps({ done: Number })` and then `const label = describe(done)`, where `describe` is a function of its own that builds a string. The parent later changes `done`. What happens to `label`?
hint: The compiler rewrites `done`, but what does `describe` receive?

choices.text: It keeps the first value
choices.why: Right. `describe` ran once with a plain number, as in lesson 2. Wrap it, `computed(() => describe(done))`, and the read happens inside a computed that follows the prop.

choices.text: Vue warns that a destructured prop was passed to a function
choices.why: There is no such warning. The code is valid; it just reads the value once.

choices.text: It follows, because a destructured prop stays reactive since Vue 3.5
choices.why: The prop stays reactive where the compiler rewrites it. `label` is computed once in the script, and nothing reruns it.

choices.text: It becomes `undefined`, because the props were destructured away
choices.why: Destructuring copied the value it had; nothing turns it into `undefined` afterwards.

prompt: In `OneWay`, the student clicks `Change the number prop` and then `Change inside the object prop`. What does the parent's line say afterwards?
hint: One of the two writes was refused.

choices.text: Parent has 35 and 35
choices.why: That would mean the number prop changed too. Assigning to `props.minutes` was refused with a warning, and the parent kept 30.

choices.text: Parent has 30 and 35
choices.why: Right. The number was refused; the property inside the object was not, and the object is the parent's own.

choices.text: Parent has 30 and 30
choices.why: That is what read-only all the way down would give, and Vue does not do that: `session.minutes` reached the parent.

choices.text: Parent has 35 and 30
choices.why: Both halves are the wrong way round: the number stayed and the object's property moved.

prompt: Why did Vue refuse `props.minutes += 5` but let `props.session.minutes += 5` through?
hint: Which object is read-only, and which object was written to?

choices.text: The props object is read-only one level deep; `session` points at the parent's own object
choices.why: Right. The child could not replace `session`, but it reached into the object `session` points at, which belongs to the parent.

choices.text: An object prop is handed to the child as a copy, so the change stays in the child and is harmless
choices.why: If it were a copy, the parent would still say 30. It says 35: the child changed the parent's data.

choices.text: Numbers are frozen by JavaScript, objects are not
choices.why: A number in a variable can be reassigned; it was Vue's read-only proxy that refused the write, not the language.

choices.text: `session` was declared as `Object`, a type Vue does not check
choices.why: The declared type is about what is passed, not about writes. The refusal comes from the props object being read-only.

prompt: A child that is given `initial` and then edits its own draft copies it once: `const draft = ___(props.initial)`.
hint: The function that makes a piece of state the child owns.

prompt: In `Emits`, the second `DoneButton` has 0 minutes, and its `done` check is `minutes > 0`. What happened when it was clicked?
hint: Read the log under the buttons as well as the warning.

choices.text: The event was dropped, and the log stayed at two lines
choices.why: The log has a third line, `s9 done, 0 minutes`. A check on an event is not a filter.

choices.text: Vue warned, and the event still reached `onDone`
choices.why: Right. `event validation failed` was printed, and `s9 done, 0 minutes` was logged anyway, as with props.

choices.text: The button was disabled by the check
choices.why: A check runs when the event is emitted; it does not touch the button.

choices.text: Vue threw an error and the page stopped updating
choices.why: There is a warning, not an error, and the page went on: the log line appeared.

prompt: A row lets the student delete a session. Which event name follows the lesson's rule?
hint: Name what the student did, not what somebody should do about it.

choices.text: `update-total`
choices.why: That names one consequence the parent might choose. The row does not know there is a total.

choices.text: `save-to-storage`
choices.why: Saving is the parent's decision, and a name like this ties the row to how the parent works today.

choices.text: `splice-sessions`
choices.why: That is an instruction about the parent's array, which the row should not know exists.

choices.text: `remove-requested`
choices.why: Right. It says what happened, and leaves the parent to decide what removing means.

prompt: A component calls `emit('click')` from its button but never declares `click`. The parent writes `<SaveButton @click="save" />`. What does one click on the button do?
hint: An undeclared event is treated as something else as well.

choices.text: Calls `save` once, from the emitted event
choices.why: That is what happens once `click` is declared. Undeclared, `@click` also becomes a native listener on the root element.

choices.text: Calls `save` twice
choices.why: Right. The undeclared `@click` fell through to the root as a native listener, and the emitted `click` reached it as the component's event too.

choices.text: Nothing, because Vue ignores an event that was not declared
choices.why: Declaring is not what lets an event through; both the emit and the native listener arrive.

choices.text: Vue refuses to compile the component until `click` is declared
choices.why: Undeclared events compile and run; the price is the fallthrough, not an error.

prompt: A parent puts `class="wide"` on a component that declares no `class` prop and has one root element. Where does the class go?
hint: It is called a fallthrough attribute.

choices.text: Into `$attrs`, until the child places it
choices.why: That is the case of a component with several roots, or one with `inheritAttrs: false`. With one root, Vue puts it there itself.

choices.text: It is lost, with a warning that the prop is unknown
choices.why:
Nothing is lost. The `Fallthrough` capture shows `class="wide"` on `GoalBar`'s `

`.

choices.text: On the root element, in place of the classes it had
choices.why: It lands on the root, but `class` merges; replacing the child's own classes would break its styling.

choices.text: On the root element, merged with the classes it already has
choices.why: Right. `class` and `style` merge with the root's own rather than replacing them.

prompt:
In the `Fallthrough` capture, which attributes appear on the `

hint: A declared prop is used by the component, not written on its element.

choices.text: `id="stats"`
choices.why: Right. `GoalBar` declares no `id`, so it fell through.

choices.text: `label="Statistics"`
choices.why: `label` is a declared prop: the component used it in its text and it is not on the element.

choices.text: `aria-describedby="help"`
choices.why: Right. It reached the root, which is how the parent tied the help text to the bar.

choices.text: `minutes="45"`
choices.why:
`minutes` is declared too, and was passed with `v-bind` as a number; it became text inside the `

`.

choices.text: `class="wide"`
choices.why:
Right. It merged with the root's classes, of which `GoalBar`'s `

` has none.

prompt: A `LabelledInput` has a `<label>` as its root and an `<input>` inside it. The parent writes `<LabelledInput placeholder="Minutes" />` and wants the placeholder on the input. What does the component need?
hint: Two pieces: one turns the default off, one says where.

choices.text: Nothing; a fallthrough attribute finds the element it belongs on
choices.why: Vue does not know which element a `placeholder` belongs on. It puts it on the root, the `<label>`, where it does nothing.

choices.text: A prop called `placeholder`, so that it stops falling through
choices.why: That works for one attribute and needs a new prop for every attribute an input accepts; the lesson's answer is to move all of them at once.

choices.text: `inheritAttrs: false` and `v-bind="$attrs"` on the `<input>`
choices.why: Right. The first stops Vue placing them on the root; the second puts them on the element they belong to.

choices.text: A second root element, so that Vue spreads the attributes over both
choices.why: With several roots, Vue warns and puts the attributes nowhere.

prompt: By the lesson's table, what is wrong with a component that needs eight props?
hint: Ask what the fewest props would be.

choices.text: It is two components, or is given state it should ask for by id
choices.why: Right. A good contract is the fewest props that let it draw itself: an id and a title, not the application's state.

choices.text: Vue refuses more than a fixed number of props
choices.why: There is no such limit. The problem is the design, not the framework.

choices.text: Its props should be grouped into one object prop so the list is shorter
choices.why: One object prop hides the same eight values and adds the risk of the last section: a child reaching into the parent's object.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as each is declared in the full form
choices.why: The full form documents and checks each prop; it does not make eight of them a clear contract.

prompt: `planned` starts at 45 in `ModelDemo`. What does the parent's line show after one press of `+15`?
hint: The child writes to the model ref, and the parent's `v-model` does the rest.

prompt: On the parent, `<MinutesField v-model="planned" />` is shorthand for what?
hint: A prop down, and an event back up.

choices.text: `:planned="planned" @change="planned = $event"`
choices.why: The names are not the variable's. Both sides agree on `modelValue` and `update:modelValue`.

choices.text: `:model-value="planned" @update:model-value="(value) => (planned = value)"`
choices.why: Right. A prop called `modelValue` and an event called `update:modelValue`, whose listener assigns.

choices.text: `:value="planned" @input="planned = $event.target.value"`
choices.why: That is `v-model` on a native `<input>`, and it hands back text; on a component it binds a prop and an event.

choices.text: `:model="planned"`, a prop the child writes to directly
choices.why: No prop is writable by the child. Writing to the model ref emits an event, and the parent assigns.

prompt: `defineModel()` with no name declares a prop called ___, and its update event.
hint: The name of the long form, in camelCase.

prompt: After the guitar session is ticked, what percentage of the weekly goal does Guitar's card show? Guitar has 20 minutes done and a goal of 90.
hint: `Math.round((done / goal) * 100)`.

prompt: Why does `SessionRow` emit `toggle` with an id instead of calling `toggleDone` itself?
hint: Who owns the list of sessions?

choices.text: `toggleDone` is not exported from `planner.js`
choices.why: `App` imports it from there, so it is exported. Where it is called is a decision about ownership.

choices.text: An emitted event is faster than a function call
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; the event ends up calling the same `toggle` function anyway.

choices.text: A component may import nothing except Vue and other components
choices.why: `SessionRow` imports `formatDay` from `planner.js`. Importing a rule is fine; changing the parent's state is what it avoids.

choices.text: The list is `App`'s; the row reports
choices.why: Right. The row has no idea a list exists or is saved; `App` replaces the list, and everything that reads it follows.

prompt: In `CourseCard`, what is the text `{{ percent }}%` inside `<progress>` for?
hint: Not every browser draws the element.

choices.text: What a browser that cannot draw `<progress>` shows instead
choices.why: Right. A browser that knows the element draws the bar; one that does not falls back to the text.

choices.text: It sets the bar's value, as `:value` does on an input
choices.why: `:value="done"` and `:max="goal"` set the bar. The text inside sets nothing.

choices.text: It is the label a screen reader reads instead of the value
choices.why: A screen reader announces the `<progress>` with its value; the text inside is not what it reads.

choices.text: A tooltip shown when the pointer rests on the bar
choices.why: A tooltip would be a `title` attribute. The text inside is the fallback content.

prompt: The student ticks the guitar session. Put what happens in order, from the click to the card.
hint: Up as an event, then down as props.

prompt: Match each need to the tool the lesson gives for it.
hint: Down, up, both, or neither.

pairs.left: A course's title, for a card to draw
The news that the student ticked a row
A field that edits a number the parent owns

prompt: A teammate wants `CourseCard` to mark its course finished, and adds a button that runs `props.done = props.goal`. What happens when it is pressed?
hint: `done` is a number, and the props object is read-only.

choices.text: The card shows 100%, and `App`'s data stays as it was
choices.why: That would be a local copy. Nothing changes at all: the write to a number prop is refused.

choices.text: It works, and the session list in `App` is marked done
choices.why: Even an accepted write would not reach the sessions: `done` is a total `App` computes from them.

choices.text: Vue warns that the target is readonly, and nothing changes
choices.why: Right. As with `Counter`'s number prop. The card should emit an event and let `App` change its own sessions.

choices.text: The compiler refuses the file, because `props` is a constant
choices.why: `const` stops `props` being reassigned, not a property being written. The refusal comes at run time, as a warning.

prompt: Which of these belong to `CourseCard`'s public contract, the part `App` relies on? Choose all that apply.
hint: The contract is what it must be given and what it can report.

choices.text: That `goal` is a required `Number`
choices.why: Right. A declared prop, with its type: `App` has to pass it.

choices.text: The `percent` it computes
choices.why: `percent` is private. It could be renamed or worked out differently without `App` noticing.

choices.text: That `planned` falls back to 0 when it is left out
choices.why: Right. A default is part of the declaration, and `App` relies on it.

choices.text: The colour its scoped style gives a paragraph
choices.why: Its markup and style are private too; they could change without anybody else noticing.
